paragraphs.title: The Psalm's Heading and Plea for Mercy

easy.explanation: He says, “O LORD, rebuke me not in thine anger.”
easy.q: What does the speaker ask the LORD not to do?

easy.explanation: He pleads, “Have mercy upon me, O LORD.”
easy.q: What does the speaker ask the LORD to have upon him?
What does the speaker say about his condition?

medium.explanation: The speaker asks not to be chastened, or disciplined, in the LORD’s hot displeasure.
medium.q: What does “chasten me” mean in this passage?

answers: He asks for mercy instead of angry rebuke and chastening
He asks for music instead of prayer
He asks for victory instead of healing
medium.explanation: The speaker asks the LORD not to rebuke or chasten him in anger and then asks for mercy.
medium.q: What is the relationship between the two requests in these verses?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to strong anger or displeasure.

answers: Humble dependence on the LORD’s mercy
Confidence in his own military power
challenge.explanation: He approaches the LORD humbly, asking for mercy and restraint from judgment.
challenge.q: What attitude does the speaker show at the beginning of the psalm?

answers: The speaker acknowledges discipline but asks that it not come in anger
The speaker denies that judgment exists
The speaker asks to punish his enemies instead of himself
challenge.explanation: He refers to rebuke and chastening but pleads that they not be given in anger.
challenge.q: How does the language of these verses balance judgment and mercy?

challenge.explanation: The speaker asks for mercy rather than rebuke in the LORD’s anger.
challenge.q: Which contrast is central to the opening plea?

paragraphs.title: Illness, Fear, and the Plea for Healing

easy.q: How does the speaker describe himself?
What does the speaker ask the LORD to do to him?
What does the speaker say is vexed?

medium.q: What does “vexed” mean in the phrase “my bones are vexed”?

answers: He has endured distress and is waiting for relief
He has no concern at all
He has already defeated his enemies
medium.explanation: The question expresses continuing suffering and a longing for the LORD’s intervention.
medium.q: What does the question “how long?” reveal about the speaker?

answers: The speaker desires the LORD’s presence and help
The speaker wants the LORD to depart forever
The speaker is calling for a musician
medium.explanation: He asks the LORD to turn toward him again and deliver him.

answers: Weakness and distress lead to requests for healing and deliverance
Victory leads to celebration and singing
Anger leads to punishment of enemies
challenge.explanation: The speaker describes his suffering and then asks for healing, return, deliverance, and salvation.
challenge.q: What progression appears in these verses?

challenge.explanation: He says, “save me for thy mercies’ sake.”
challenge.q: On what basis does the speaker ask to be saved?

answers: His bones are vexed and his soul is sore vexed
His body is strong and his soul is joyful
His body is healed and his soul is at peace
challenge.explanation: The passage mentions vexed bones and a soul that is “sore vexed.”
challenge.q: How are the speaker’s body and soul both affected?

paragraphs.title: The Argument Against Death and the Flood of Tears

easy.explanation: He says, “For in death there is no remembrance of thee.”
easy.q: What does the speaker say is absent in death?

answers: Who shall give the LORD thanks there
Who shall lead the music there
easy.explanation: He asks, “in the grave who shall give thee thanks?”
easy.q: What does the speaker ask about the grave?

easy.explanation: He says, “all the night make I my bed to swim.”
easy.q: What does the speaker say he makes his bed do?

answers: He wants to remain alive so that he may remember and thank the LORD
He believes death will bring him greater wealth
He wants to escape all prayer
medium.explanation: He points to remembrance and thanksgiving as reasons to ask for deliverance from death.
medium.q: What is the speaker’s argument concerning death?

answers: His sighing and sorrow have exhausted him
He is pleased with his singing
medium.explanation: His continual groaning has left him weary.
medium.q: What does “I am weary with my groaning” mean?

answers: His tears water his couch and make his bed swim
He sleeps peacefully through the night
medium.explanation: He says, “I water my couch with my tears.”
medium.q: How does the speaker describe his nighttime grief?

answers: He asks for life so he can continue remembering and thanking the LORD
He asks to be hidden from all worship
He asks to become a warrior after death
challenge.explanation: The speaker argues that death would prevent the remembrance and thanksgiving he offers to God.
challenge.q: What is the central appeal behind the speaker’s reference to death?

answers: His bed swimming and his couch watered with tears
His enemies singing in the streets
challenge.explanation: The images of a bed swimming and a couch watered with tears portray overwhelming grief.
challenge.q: Which image most strongly emphasizes the amount of the speaker’s sorrow?

challenge.explanation: The speaker describes exhaustion, groaning, and tears throughout the night.
challenge.q: What emotional pattern dominates these verses?

paragraphs.title: The Enemies, the Heard Prayer, and Confidence in Deliverance

answers: It is consumed because of grief
easy.explanation: He says, “Mine eye is consumed because of grief.”
easy.q: What has happened to the speaker’s eye?

easy.explanation: The speaker says, “Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity.”

answers: The voice of the speaker’s weeping
easy.explanation: He says, “the LORD hath heard the voice of my weeping.”

answers: It grows weak or worn with age and grief
medium.explanation: The phrase describes an eye weakened and worn down by grief and enemies.
medium.q: What does “waxeth old” mean in the phrase about the speaker’s eye?

answers: Because the LORD has heard his weeping
Because they have come to heal him
medium.explanation: The command is followed by the reason that the LORD has heard his weeping.
medium.q: Why does the speaker tell the workers of iniquity to depart?

answers: The LORD hears the prayer, receives it, and the enemies are told to retreat
The speaker celebrates, becomes ill, and then prays
The enemies heal the speaker and then depart
medium.explanation: The speaker declares that the LORD has heard and will receive his prayer, then calls for his enemies to withdraw.
medium.q: What order of events appears in the closing verses?

answers: He moves from grief and weakness to confidence that his prayer has been heard
He moves from joy to fear of death
He moves from victory to illness
challenge.explanation: After describing grief, he confidently declares that the LORD has heard and will receive his prayer.
challenge.q: What major change occurs in the speaker’s condition?

answers: They should be ashamed, sore vexed, and return suddenly
They should heal him and join him
They should lead him in music
challenge.explanation: He asks that his enemies be ashamed, troubled, and forced to turn back.
challenge.q: What does the speaker want to happen to his enemies?

answers: It enables him to command evildoers to depart and expect their retreat
It causes him to join the evildoers
It makes him stop speaking to the LORD
challenge.explanation: Because he trusts that the LORD has heard his prayer, he can confront his enemies with confidence.
challenge.q: How does confidence in prayer affect the speaker’s response to his enemies?
